utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I should like to begin by tendering into evidence, and I should like the usher to distribute the list of the staff of the health centre in Vitez that we spoke about yesterday. It has been translated.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be marked D19/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) This is the document we discussed yesterday, we finished, and we just added the English translation. May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Kovacic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mujezinovic. I hope you had a good rest after yesterday. Now, will you please -- and let us try to be as brief as possible, because we have only half an hour to complete this, so will you please answer me just "yes" or "no," just to speed matters up. After you left the room in which you saw Cerkez and other persons that you mentioned, and then you went back after working on the statement with Cilic, did you see Cerkez in the building again that night?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, early in the morning, there was a meeting with Mr. Santic and Mr. Skopljak and you and other colleagues that you had invited from the cellar; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that meeting, you talked, and on one side there were eminent Bosniak citizens from Vitez, and on the other side were Mr. Santic and Mr. Skopljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and Zvonko and -- Jozic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So it was Jozic and Cilic who also attended the meeting in addition to Santic and Skopljak. You perceived Santic and Skopljak as representatives of the civilian structure of the HVO; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As the representatives of HDZ politics in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we then move on to something else. As a physician, and as a physician who is under legal obligation, and you were even called an HVO physician, have you had an opportunity of examining the internees in the cinema except on that occasion when you said that you had to go and choose the negotiators?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't really understand what you mean by "internees."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean people who were imprisoned in the cinema, that is, in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember a case, his jaw was broken, and he was in the cinema. There was a commission set up which went there and examined those detained people. I was not on that commission. It was Dr. Enisa Mulalic, Rado Savanovic, Dr. Tibold, were its members. I don't know who else, but I did not go there to that location to examine them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: May I now tender another document. There is a note about that examination, so I should like to look at that. Will the usher please help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, could you have a look at that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the upper right corner, it is handwritten, but in capital letters, "Tibold, Dr. Franjo." Is that the doctor that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recognise his signature? I suppose you knew it because you worked together as doctors and exchanged documentations.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was a director for a while, and this is his signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is his signature?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we have the title down there which you have just mentioned, president of the medical commission of the HVO, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I suppose he was, but I don't really know which one. There was -- Franjo was more experienced; he was an epidemiologist. It is quite possible that he was the president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Doctor, tell us, since on the top of that sheet, right below the first line, it says "Mensus Aganovic," and then it is indicated "went home," and somebody's signature. And then it says, "Send home 26th of April." Do you know, have you had the opportunity of seeing or hearing one of those people? Were they really released, some of the people from that list? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Will you tell me -- whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean all of them, any one from 1 to 22. Only the one on the top has nothing to do with this, evidently.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I was in the cellar, I called Zvonko Cilic. I knew all those people, and I knew their diagnosis, and I did recommend that some 20 of them be released, because they were chronic patients, and the conditions there were impossible. And I told also Dr. Franjo Tibold, but I really do not know which one of them was released. I know that Dr. Enisa Mulalic refused to go on working because they would not accept her recommendations. She was a Muslim and worked in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So you advised that some be released because you knew them. Does any of those names figure here, or were they 20 others?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, for instance, Latif Dzoferovic suffered from tuberculosis or, rather, chronic bronchitis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you give us just the number?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is Number 1 on the list. Zijad Puric, number 10, he had heart valves implanted. Safet Malkic, 11, was suffering from gout. Alihodja Atif was suffering from asthma, from -- number 12, he was suffering from asthma. Fikret Kablar, it was -- he was in a post-infarction period. He is a young man. It is number 15. Harun Sulevic, number 18, formerly suffered from a stroke. We say that he suffered from a cerebrovascular insult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So there are various patients of that kind. Another question related to this document --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dr. Jusuf Mehmedovic also suffered from severe bronchitis and was allergic to all medicines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is number 22?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But will you just keep the document, please, for a while. Look at this paper down below 22 at the bottom. It says "approved," and then the signature looks like "Pero Skopljak." Do you know Pero Skopljak's signature, since you saw documents that he perhaps signed and worked with him? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I guess this is Pero Skopljak's signature. After all, seven years have passed by, but I suppose that is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Usher, you can take these documents away from the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, will you please tell us, when you left Vitez and went to Zenica, did you have any contact with your wife, I mean by telephone, because she had stayed in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but only from the police station, that is, the civilian police station in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, she called from the civilian police station?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. She called me once from a Croat woman and told me that all -- that the telephone was being bugged and that somebody was listening to all that she was saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell us, Doctor, did she ever call you or did you call her? But I suppose it was she who called you perhaps from the building of the Workers' University, from the command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My wife told me that she had tried to talk to Pero Skopljak and Mario Cerkez, and that Mario Cerkez told her that I was no man at all, how could I leave the family, and what had I done, I mean, to leave and to leave my family back in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he allowed her to telephone?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think it was Mario Cerkez. I think she told me that it was another Croat, Markisa Rujic, who took her into his office and allowed her to call me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she perhaps tell you that Zvonko Cilic organised it so that she could call you from the command?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, she told me that Mirko Samija, who was the chief of the civilian police in Vitez, was the one who made it possible for her to make her call from the civilian police in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since we're on this subject, why did you leave your family and go to Zenica? Yes, you told us how it was, but still how did you -- where did you find the courage to do it, since you must have been aware and you told us that considerable chaos reigned in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I received threats, and I said that [indiscernible], the man who told me that, that there was an order to have me killed, I told him that I could not leave the Vitez --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I object to that question for the same reasons as the information was attempted to be elicited on direct examination. In cross-examination, it doesn't make the evidence any more or less reliable, Your Honour, and we're not bound by any questions, I believe, that Mr. Kovacic asks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, counsel has a point. Do you want to pursue this line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, actually I think that it wasn't a question problem. The answer was the problem, because the witness is not answering the question. But I can put it a different way. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please let us not get into these procedural problems. Will you tell me another thing? Was that the first threat that you received, just "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first threat?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first threat ever since I began to work there again on the 19th of April onward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the first threat in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that there was a verbal threat, but nothing particular, but that was the first serious threat which was communicated to me directly, tête-à-tête.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So you went to Zenica. Edib Zlotrg, you said he was a liaison officer. Was he involved in the exchange?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes. Thank you. Could we now see video 2, please? (In English) Let us play one short excerpt. It's about 10 or 15 seconds, just the one scene I would like the witness to recognise, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has he got a transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There's no text, just a picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Play the video. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, I thought you said there was no text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is the picture we need, so it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the rest is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. You want it to be played from here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right, and I would like the technician to slow down the text, because there is a comment which has nothing to do with it, with the scene we see. He's talking about hospitals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. Well, let them know what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Enough. We saw what we wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise, we saw it yesterday, also the building of the craft centre where you had the health centre; was that it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recognise this damage done to the roof? Was it an explosion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I was there, there was no damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this didn't happen while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you then afterwards hear that the roof of the building was hit?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard that a shell had fallen in the vicinity, in the neighbourhood of that building, but I heard about it when the war was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this craft centre is in the heart of the town?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that whole centre is within that block of buildings. Well, I mean it is a craft centre, so it is -- there were many shops there, and I heard that a coffee shop had been hit during the war. But I learned about that later, that in that block of buildings or outlets, one shop had been hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Just one more question, and that will be it. I'm referring to the communication of the coordinating committee, and I'm not going into it, but it referred to the language that was to be used in schools. Do you know what I'm referring to, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So will you please tell me just one thing? Which language, that is, the previous school year, which language was used in schools in the municipality of Vitez during the previous school year?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that language was called Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Croato-Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, was there some form of that common language, if I may say so, in the territory of the former Yugoslavia which was used in Bosnia? Was there another official name to refer to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Formerly, the authorities -- that is, prior to 1990, the authorities did not approve officially that it be called the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, thank you. And will you tell us, please, textbooks, school textbooks, were evidently books which were published during the SFRY which no longer existed, which had become obsolete; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, textbooks were published, as far as I know, because I'm not an educator and I did not really pay much attention to that. But there was the publishing house Svijetlost, in Sarajevo. There were the curricula adopted by the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina applicable throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell us, did you have an opportunity to hear that people were protesting against those textbooks, which were crammed with facts and knowledge about the former Yugoslavia and so on and so forth? Were people protesting against it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Do you mean educators?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean not only educators, all the educated people, I mean all the people involved with education. Your children are already big. I mean they are out of school.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that is not true. My son is now 18 and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, did you, as a parent --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I do think there were some protests, but I don't really know much about that. I know that some people were against it. I think that sometime in September, the HVO introduced the curriculum of the Republic of Croatia in Vitez, and I know that the Bosniak side protested against that. Also, a teacher, Arifa Tunovic, was killed in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's stick to our topic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And, no, I mean because of linguistic problems, because she was the teacher of the mother tongue. And from what I heard, I think she refused to switch to the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, right. But will you please just confirm the following or deny? The textbooks that existed at the time, and we're referring to 1993, they were obviously published during the ex-Yugoslavia, which at that time did not exist and which was the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really don't know if all the textbooks were published, so in all likelihood, they all were published then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, just wait. Do you really believe that during that chaos of 1992, any textbook would be published in the territory of Bosnia or Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe this was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Okay, Doctor. Thank you very much for your testimony, and I'm sorry if I bored you, but you've come here to help all of us. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have no further questions. Cross-examined by Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Mujezinovic. My name is Steve Sayers, and I'm from Alexandria, Virginia. I represent Dario Kordic, and I have just a few questions for you today. Since I'm not speaking in your language, I don't want to give the interpreters fits, and I've been told that I tend to speak a little quickly, so it would help if you would answer the questions "Yes" or "No," or as short as possible, and we'll be through with you as soon as we can. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, Dr. Mujezinovic, you've actually given four separate statements to the Prosecutors over the course of your involvement with these cases, spanning, it looks like, a four-year period.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first statement you gave on March the 1st, 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I made this first statement in 1993. I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The first one that we have from you is actually dated March the 1st, 1995, Dr. Mujezinovic. Are you saying that you actually made an earlier statement to the Prosecutors in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you give a statement to in 1993, then?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: To the investigators of the Tribunal from The Hague, from this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was in 1993, was it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, in 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That was just a translation error. The second statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor was over a three-day period from January 13th -- sorry, July the 13th to July the 16th, 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, I gave three statements in the course of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We only have two of them. The second one that we have is from July the 13th through July the 16th, 1995. Do you recall giving statements to the Prosecutors during that period of time and having them reduced to writing and actually signing that statement as a truthful and accurate version of what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I was extremely dissatisfied with the translation into Bosnian, and I requested certain corrections to be made, which were never made or, rather, I don't know whether they were made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you signed that statement as being factually accurate, didn't you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but in agreement that corrections be made, because I was not satisfied with the translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, when did you make those corrections to the incorrect statement that you had signed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether any corrections were made to that inaccurate statement, sir, ever?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The next statement you gave to the Prosecutors was on February the 3rd of 1997; right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that as far as I can remember, it was in 1995. I think there were three statements, but I'm not sure; two or three.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe the Trial Chamber has been presented with an assembled package of all of your statements, Dr. Mujezinovic, and one of them, the third one, in fact, is actually dated February the 3rd of 1997. Do you remember giving that statement to Mr. Gregory Kehoe, assisted by Lejla Avdagic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that I made a statement in 1997 in the office of the Tribunal in Sarajevo, in 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was actually a few months before you gave testimony in the Blaskic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't point out the factual errors that were contained in your July 1995 statement in that February the 3rd, 1997 statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was always complaining about it. Two days ago, I complained here that the translation wasn't good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fourth written statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, Dr. Mujezinovic, was six months after you had testified in the Blaskic case, and it was given on March the 14th, 1998, to an individual named Spork; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. If that is what it says, it's probably correct. As far as I can remember, I made statements in '95 and '97.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it assist you to see the statement that you signed on March the 14th, 1998, to jog your memory as to whether you had actually made that statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I believe you already have the English and the Croatian, and I have an extra copy here for the witness, if that would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness have the copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next question, Dr. Mujezinovic: Is that an accurate copy of your signature on the bottom of the first page of the English version of your March the 14th, 1998, statement to the Prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't point out the factual inaccuracies in the July 1995 statement to the Prosecutors anywhere in that statement, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I must repeat once again that I did complain of the poor quality of the translations, and I don't know what it says here in the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, in the Blaskic case, on August the 20th, 1997, being shown a copy of your July 1995 statement by Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. This was two years ago. I think I spent three days in the courtroom. I was shown quite a number of these texts in the courtroom, as I have been shown yesterday and today, my statements, video recordings. I don't know exactly what he showed me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps we can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With the Trial Chamber's permission, I have actually prepared little excerpt of the relevant cross-examination on this particular statement, and I think it will be of great assistance to the Trial Chamber in evaluating the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, what is it that this is leading to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's leading to this, Your Honour, if I can just precise this: Basically, Mr. Hayman pointed out that there was a reference made in the July 1995 statement that Dr. Mujezinovic had supposedly given, and he pointed out in that statement that Mr. Darko Kraljevic, supposedly, was being treated by him as a result of a drug-induced psychosis, that he was suffering from an overdose of cocaine, and that treatment was given to him in that regard. That's exactly what the statement says on page 4, I believe. Dr. Mujezinovic, when confronted with that statement, it was said -- I think he used the word "absurd," factually inaccurate, that he pointed out that inaccuracy to the Prosecutor's representatives who had actually taken that statement and was told, "Don't worry about it." If I may, I'd just like to address a question to the witness to see if that jogs his memory at all about that particular exchange, and if it doesn't, I have the relevant exchange here in black and white for him to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has heard what it is that you are going to put, and perhaps he can deal with it straightaway. Do you remember that, Doctor, being put in the Blaskic trial, and giving those answers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I said at the time that we doctors may suspect something, but in order to prove it, and to establish a firm diagnosis, we need to have sound arguments. I may have had my doubts, but I wasn't absolutely specific about it, and I did not say this. I complained about it. I also said that no nurse could make such a statement either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, since that goes to an issue in the case, I would like to have this exchange marked as an exhibit for future reference, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D16/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you read or understand English at all, Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I understand English to be able to read medical literature, but I know very little English, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Dr. Mujezinovic. You actually pointed out on page 1816 that the translation was, in your view, absurd?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where is this in our transcripts, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think it's page 1816, Your Honour. If you take a look at -- the page numbers are actually in the middle of the pages; it's actually three pages in. The answer begins on Line 21.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I think the point you were making, Dr. Mujezinovic, and correct me if I'm wrong, but the point you were making to the Prosecutors is, when you saw this, you actually told them that this was an incorrect factual statement, this statement that was supposedly contained in the statement regarding Mr. Darko Kraljevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I have already said that I protested, but it is customary in medicine for us to have a working diagnosis, but to be able to have an exact diagnosis, it is not customary except if we have some firm confirmation: Laboratory tests, EKG, x-rays, ultrasound tests, and so on. Only once we have those tests can we establish the official diagnosis. I didn't have a laboratory to be able to make those tests. I may have had my suspicions, because my colleagues suspected, as I said, that this was a heart attack, but it obviously was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, Dr. Mujezinovic. I think that we are like two ships passing in the night here a little bit. I think my question was, had you pointed this factual inaccuracy out to the Prosecutors before you were actually asked to sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I complained to the Prosecutors about the translation and explained that I could not have said that explicitly. I didn't say what I saw written, and as far as I can remember, the Prosecution told me that the corrections would be made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they ever were?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that that statement had actually been presented to the Trial Chamber and referred to in a road map of your testimony, at least what the Office of the Prosecutor expected your testimony to be, without those corrections having been made?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that an uncorrected copy of your July 1995 statement had been presented to the Trial Chamber and referred to in a little outline of what the Prosecutor had expected your testimony to be?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I denied that in the courtroom, and I said what I have just said to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's move on a little. You were asked some questions by the Prosecutor about this fellow, Darko Kraljevic, and the HOS troops that he commanded. And in response to a question from Judge Bennouna, I believe, you made reference to the fact that the HOS was the military arm of a party called the Croatian Party of Rights, or the HSP. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do. As far as I know, that was the military arm of the Croatian Party of Rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And the HSP is a completely distinct and separate political party from the HDZ; you would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not familiar with the programme, but they are two different parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did I understand you to say that you treated Mr. Kraljevic prior to the time that you acquired these statements that you've related to the Trial Chamber, you treated him for suspected alcohol toxicity by intravenous injections of the drug diazepam?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't put it like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you treat him for suspected alcohol toxicity with the drug diazepam, sir? "Yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that he was given diazepam intramuscularly and that he was given an injection for detoxification with alcohol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The trade name of diazepam is actually Valium, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Diazepam. I don't know whether it's called valium in America. We call it diazepam or apaurin. I don't know what its name is in America.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the point is it's a central nervous system depressant, isn't it, just like alcohol?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it's a drug to treat anxiety, which relaxes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one would feel, within a short period of time from having been injected with this drug, a sense of euphoria; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you stated, sir, that it was in the course of these sessions when he was having injections -- and I'm quoting now from page 50 of the LiveNote, at lines 15 to 22: In the course of these sessions when he was having injections, then he would relate to you the conversations that he was having with Messrs. Skopljak, Valenta, and Cerkez. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said, that he was particularly referring to Pero Skopljak and Anto Valenta, and yesterday I said that he would occasionally talk to Cerkez as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, let's get to the heart of the matter. In your view, this gentleman was psychologically unstable, explosive, I believe, to use your word. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that he could be explosive at times, that his moods would change, that he was a man who was unpredictable, his reactions were unpredictable, and in my opinion, I said that he was rather unstable, that he didn't have a firm character, in the sense that if he took a decision, that he would really stick to it. This was a young man, full of strength and energy, and he wanted to assert himself. That is my understanding of him. A good-looking young man, well built, physically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you remember testifying two years ago that this was not a stable person psychologically? "With such people you cannot foresee what their next reaction will be. He was psychologically unstable, explosive"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For two days I have been repeating the same thing. I really don't know what you want of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You agree that you did say that two years ago, in the Blaskic case, when you were talking on the subject of Mr. Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if Mr. Sayers could provide the page reference. It's not in the transcript that he has provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, I can show the witness the pages I want. It's page 1826 and 1827 of the Blaskic trial transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Sayers, we can get through this as rapidly as possible. There's no need to put to the witness whether he remembers saying things. He may well not. It's perfectly understandable. If you want to refer to specific items in the evidence, you can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't want to waste time and flog a dead horse, Your Honour, in the interest of expediency, but let me just see if I can jog his memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember saying, sir, in response to cross-examination on August the 21st, that Mr. Kraljevic was not a stable person psychologically?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that in my opinion, he was an unstable person. In my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you agree that you gave that testimony two years ago?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, I said that in my opinion, he was an unstable person of whom you never knew how he would react at a particular time. That was my opinion as a doctor, as a man, as an individual, as far as I knew him. Allow me to say that I knew Darko Kraljevic just as somebody from Vitez, a young, well-built man who wanted to be important. I didn't have much contact with him. I didn't treat him before. I went to treat his family members, his grandmother, grandfather, but Darko Kraljevic had not consulted me, at least, for any health problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, it's true, isn't it, that the troops under the command of this psychologically stable (sic) or explosive individual were responsible for much of the criminal activity, at least in your view, that was going on in Vitez in the first -- over the latter half of 1992 and the first part of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, there has to be an order for all military operations. Now, who issued the orders, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall, sir, giving testimony either yesterday or the day before to the effect that at some point, the HOS troops became incorporated into the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they changed their name. They became a special purpose unit called the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And this was announced in public, on local television, that Darko Kraljevic had been promoted to the commander of that unit with the rank of colonel. Until then, as far as I can recollect, people were not going around with ranks. There were former JNA officers -- we mentioned one of them yesterday, Filipovic. I think he was a Lieutenant-Colonel in the former JNA, or a Major, I'm not quite sure -- but in any event, then there was Ramiz Dugalic in Vitez who was a major in the former JNA. There were captains who came and said that they held such-and-such a rank. Regarding ranks, this was the first time I heard that ranks were being introduced into the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you would agree, doctor, that these were turbulent times, both from a military perspective and a perspective of society in general, with the break-up of the former communist state of Yugoslavia, the secession of various constituent republics, and a state of civil war being threatened in the first part of 1991; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the first half of '91?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was war in Croatia then, and in Vitez, we were afraid that it might spill over into Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time, and I said so yesterday, the crisis staff was set up in Vitez precisely because of that, because the immediate danger of war and difficulties with communications, difficulties with regular supplies of citizens, and the situation was difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's try to approach this chronologically. It's true, I believe, that the Croats and the Muslims voted overwhelmingly at a national referendum held on February the 29th, 1992, and March the 1st, 1992, in favour of the establishment of a newly independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct? You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this newly independent state, sir, was born in an atmosphere of impending civil war, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the Serb Democratic Party in the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, its president, threatened -- we saw it on television -- he threatened that if Bosnia and Herzegovina were recognised as an independent state or republic, then the Serb people would not accept that and that they would fight against it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe that the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina was declared to be independent on March the 3rd of 1991, just two days after the conclusion of the national referendum; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Possibly. I know it was the former half of 1991, after the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when the Croats and Muslims, Bosniaks, voted almost 100 per cent for an autonomous republic. There were also some Serbs, but very few and far between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think I may have misspoken, Dr. Mujezinovic. I said 1991, but it was actually 1992, wasn't it, when the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was declared?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I don't think -- it was '92, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may, I just have a few documents that I would like to go over with you that track fairly chronologically, and I have put together these documents in chronological order for the Bench, the Prosecutor, you, and co-counsel, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the documents be placed on the ELMO, please, for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The bundle will be marked D17/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, we were saying to the Registrar that it really is very hot in here, and I suspect that everybody is feeling it. Therefore, we've requested to move to the other court, and we'll see if we can do it by the break, if possible, or after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I thought I was experiencing the signs of premature ageing, Your Honour, in all candour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first document, Dr. Mujezinovic, just to bring the Trial Chamber up to speed, appears to be a decree issued by the presidency of the brand-new State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, within actually about a month of its establishment, with a state of imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could it be placed on the ELMO, please, for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Usher, if you would place that on the ELMO for the interpreters, I've just received a request for that, although we're not going to spend very much time on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's really only one question, Dr. Mujezinovic. You do recall this decree being issued by the presidency of the newly-independent republic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me see. Yes, I do remember. It was announced on television, broadcast on radio. There was a lot of talk about it at the time. I mean it wasn't only me who knew about this. Any person who could read and write and who would listen knew about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I totally agree with that. In April of 1992, that's when Sarajevo was surrounded and the town of Bijeljina was attacked by Serbian forces; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but it is correct that Sarajevo was attacked, and Bijeljina too, 1992. The first half; April, most probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that as of April of 1992 and proceeding throughout, really, the rest of 1992 and 1993, notwithstanding your views as to the previous ethnic harmony, if you like, between the three constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the decades before, a state of vicious civil war existed? You would have to agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the time in Vitez, we did not -- or I personally did not have that feeling. At official meetings, there was a danger of conflicts breaking out because that threat had been pronounced in the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not just talking on the municipal level of Vitez, Dr. Mujezinovic. I'm taking a bit more of a broader view than that, a national view. It would be fair to say that throughout your country, within a month of its establishment, a vicious civil war was unleashed by one of the ethnic minorities in that country upon the other two ethnic minorities; that would be fair to say, and you would have to agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we've dealt with that. Mr. Sayers, that question is really a matter of argument and comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I will move on swiftly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would. You did tell us yesterday you would be half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I know, and I feel great recrimination for that. I don't want to mislead the Bench in the least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked a question yesterday about refugees, Dr. Mujezinovic. Do you know what the population of the town of Vitez was in 1991, according to the census?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the population of the municipality was some 20.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, actually the population of the town itself was 7.200, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thereabouts, yes, the urban part of it is not more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as I understand the response that you made, I believe, to questions from the Bench, from the autumn of 1991 and throughout 1992 and 1993, refugees came flooding into the central Lasva Valley from the east, from the west, and from the north.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I said yesterday that the first refugees arrived from East Croatia, and they were Croats, and subsequently Bosniak Muslims began to arrive from East Bosnia in Vitez. More specifically, we had them from Tjentiste. That was from Foca, then from Zenica, from Sipovo, that is, the western part of Bosnia. In Vitez, we had refugees -- I mean Muslims from those places. Yesterday, I also said that from Rogatica, and my wife came from there, about 20 refugees were accommodated in the house where I lived in Vitez, and they spent almost nine months in my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, 25.000 refugees actually left the town of Jajce when it fell to Serbian attacks at the end of October of 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was the end of October, November. I examined those people, both Croats and Muslims, and I did examine them in this reserve location of the health centre. I had heard that there were some 7.000 Croats from Jajce, but I really do not remember how many Muslims there were, because there were other people who were responsible for keeping a record of that. Yesterday, I said that the overwhelming majority of Croats left Vitez. Not very many of them stayed there. They asked to go to Croatia, to go to Tomislavgrad, but by and large to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a prominent citizen in the community, Dr. Mujezinovic, you would agree with me, I take it, that this massive influx of refugees put a tremendous strain upon the local resources that you had available, both in terms of housing, food, medical care, and other resources too.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Excuse me. My family -- I just told you that in my household, there were 20 refugees, so naturally that we were put under it -- the whole municipality and all the households had -- the expenditures rose steeply, of course. The standard of living began to drop, because as I was saying, my family had five members, and all of a sudden there were 20 people more at home in my household. We were all trying. At that time, I, I mean as a doctor, was trying to help all those people, to help them, to put them up somewhere, to not let them sleep in the park, in the open, regardless of their ethnic origin. But it is quite true that there was an enormous -- a tremendous influx of refugees from Jajce, and I believe it was late October or perhaps early November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And using your own personal experience, I think you would agree and you would tell the Trial Chamber that the strain that that put on available housing in the area was absolutely tremendous.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Why? I already stated where we accommodated those people; mostly in private homes, those who had their relatives there, and in summer cottages, and there were quite a number of those in the villages of Kruscica, Ahmici, Hrasno. There were a number of such cottages, and mostly people from Zenica -- I mean people living in Zenica had those cottages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, that brings us to the October 1992 blockade at Ahmici that you talked about. That was immediately before the fall of Jajce, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I said that at the time, I was not in Vitez, that I spent my weekends working in the Travnik Hospital. It was only on Monday morning that I learned of a roadblock in Ahmici, that is, the main regional road to Split and Banja Luka. In point of fact, we do not have any other road except for the one that goes to Doboj or, rather, to Croatia. There were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Doctor, let me interrupt you. If you deal with these matters shortly, I hope we can finish more quickly. Mr. Sayers, we have been over this ground. Unless there's something new you want to ask, I suggest we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a couple of cleanup questions on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree that in the autumn of 1992, sir, there were more people wearing uniforms than there were not in the population generally; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What year are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were informed that Mr. Dzemal Merdan from the 3rd Corps command in Zenica had actually ordered that roadblock to be installed in Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but that is something that I learned at a later date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the hostilities, sir, and I appreciate that you don't know about them because you didn't observe them first-hand, but you and the political leadership in Vitez cooperated by going on television and trying to calm down the tensions that were created as a result of that fighting; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yesterday, I said that with two local priests and Pero Skopljak, that we all appeared on the local television, sometime in the evening of the 23rd, in an attempt to calm down the situation in Vitez and explain what it was all about. Munib Kajmovic was also supposed to go, but he had called me and told me that he could not, and asked me if I could go in his stead, so I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going to the second document in the bundle, by the time of the October conflict --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we must give these a number. The first had better be 17/1.1, and the second 17/1.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, before you continue, I just want to have a clarification on the answer that was given to your question that there were more people wearing uniforms than there were not in the population generally. I would just like to have an explanation of that. Exactly what does that mean? There were more uniformed persons than there were civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Judge Robinson. That was not a question that was characterised by a phenomenal amount of artistry, and I'll see if I can clear it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Dr. Mujezinovic, in response to Judge Robinson's question, that there were more civilians, more male civilians, people of military age, who were actually wearing uniforms in the latter half of 1992 than were actually wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, and yesterday I think some evidence was shown, that there were many conscripts in uniforms of the HVO, the Territorial Defence, the HOS also in the first half. There were quite a number of men wearing uniforms. At the time, I would go through by car, and I saw them in the streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as you were driving through the streets, just to follow up on this, you would see more people in uniform than out of uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Let me tell you. In the town itself, to the best of my knowledge and memory, the Territorial Defence or, rather, the staff of the Territorial Defence at that time was sending units in the direction of Sarajevo and Vlasic, and I also heard at the time that the HVO was also sending its units to Vlasic. So in the town itself, as these units were being sent also to the ground, there were not very many of them. There were uniformed individuals, but those units were being sent out to the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Sayers, I believe that this line of questioning is leading us nowhere. Could you go on to something else, because this is leading nowhere. You know how much time is valuable, and everybody's time, including that of the accused. So we have to go further. We don't see what this all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I take that and will try to move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning your attention to Exhibit D17/1.2, do you recognise this as the decree issued on June the 20th, 1992, declaring a state of war in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Sayers, I wonder about the point of this. You're presenting this witness with a whole lot of documents which he's not even seen, and I've been going through it and I got halfway through, I got to 9 or 10. I don't know how many documents there are in all. Is this the appropriate witness, first of all, to put these documents to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It may be, Your Honour, because he was a prominent political figure in Vitez and the president of the war presidency, which had, according to his testimony, military power or the power to issue orders to the army, and I would have thought that he would be the appropriate witness to authenticate or to identify this kind of document. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. But let us do it more quickly. Because of the time this witness has been giving evidence, which is already over two days, it had been hoped that we could go fairly quickly. I would also ask you to bear in mind that relying on the estimates we were given yesterday, arrangements would have been made for witnesses to come here, and we need to get through those witnesses this week. So I'm afraid there will be a time limit on the amount available for questioning. Perhaps you can go through fairly quickly with the witness. Ask him if he can remember the documents or not, number them, and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I interrupt for this purpose only? Of course, if the Defence choose to present me with a bundle of documents, inviting me to admit them, I'll deal with it and they can be dealt with compendiously. It's a matter I was going to raise this afternoon, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You mean if you had a chance to look at these documents, --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I haven't had a chance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- it may be possible to admit them over the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, probably, but certainly if we're given generally advance notice, we can admit documents and they can then be incorporated into the core bundle and so on. Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, and that would be much more helpful, because as it is, we're going to have to go between the two bundles to pick these documents up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can deal with that this afternoon in our procedural discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sayers, what I suggest is this: We'll adjourn now for our usual break. We'll make it half an hour, because everyone has got to move. Will you please discuss these matters with Mr. Nice, see if it's possible for the documents all to be admitted and numbered, and then there may not be any need to put them to the witness unless there are specific matters you want to raise with him? In that way, I hope that we can finish his evidence as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Sayers, we have to add that the submission of documents has to have some connection with the testimony itself. This has to be linked with the testimony that was given. There has to be a relationship, because we cannot have the witness coming to testify on a given point, go the full range of all kinds of things. It has to be linked to the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: May I, please? Your Honours, may I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the fourth day I'm spending in this courtroom, not the second day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got that in mind. That's why we're trying to finish and get you home. Well, if the break could be spent profitably, we'll sit again at quarter to 11.00 (sic) and with a view to having this witness finished within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll meet again in courtroom 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have conferred with Mr. Nice over the break, and the documents that we have presented to the Trial Chamber I believe are not objectionable to the Prosecution. They consist of three things. The first two documents are official documents from the official published lists of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; the other category of documents are documents that are within the Prosecution's own core bundle, and the other category of documents are documents that exist and were introduced as exhibits in Blaskic. Your Honours, mindful of your injunction that this gentleman has been testifying for four days, and with your permission, I'm not going to go through those with him. I would like to finish up this cross-examination with about ten minutes of questions on topics which were directly covered by this gentleman in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, you testified that you assumed the chairman of the war presidency on February the 2nd, 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That made you the leader of the Muslim community in Vitez at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that gave you supreme authority in the municipality along with your colleagues on the war presidency, and that included control over the army; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, we had no translation to the question, "That made you the leader of the Muslim community in Vitez."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It did make you the leader of the Muslim community in Vitez, did it not, Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I became president of the war presidency, a body that was taking decisions, passing orders, recommendations, conclusions, and we implemented everything we received from the presidency and government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (Microphone not activated) ... control over the Muslim military forces in your area; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The military forces in Vitez and the police could not undertake any action without our approval.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And as chairman of the war presidency, Dr. Mujezinovic, you were fully informed about the numbers of troops, equipment, and dispositions of the TO troops in the Vitez area? You testified about that just last Friday in the Kupreskic case, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were provided with the exact deployments and dispositions of each of the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Territorial Defence within your area; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had the deployment and disposition of the HVO units as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, sir, but you knew about -- there's no question that you knew about the dispositions of the TO and ABiH units in Vitez before April the 16th, 1993, outbreak of hostilities. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we had to report all military facilities to UNPROFOR, and the location of all armed forces, and this was reported by members of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the BiH army actually had wartime units in Stari Vitez prior to the outbreak of hostilities in the middle of April; that is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had the defence staff in Stari Vitez, and the deployment of the brigade that we had was not stationed in Stari Vitez, only the Defence headquarters of Vitez, the commander of which was Sefkjia Dzidic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the army had units in the surrounding villages, such as Kruscica, Preocica, and Poculica; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is right. Only those units were mobile, and they went to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were all units of the 325th Mountain Brigade; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that brigade actually included men from the villages of Santici, Pirici, and Ahmici as well, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, military conscripts, and I already said that all able-bodied adults were either in the army or in the defence staff or in the police or in the civil defence, which meant the entire population had certain assignments, because the danger of war had been declared, and there was a kind of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. And that included men who lived in the villages that I just mentioned: Santici, Pirici, and Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as president of the war presidency throughout 1993 and 1994, what personal responsibility or duty did you have to ensure that criminals who had been apprehended, and were within the judicial system being prosecuted, actually had their cases disposed of? Did you have any responsibility to do that once the criminal investigation had begun?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The war presidency had, as I said, it issued orders, conclusions, and recommendations, and the order was that all criminals, if any, as well as those who did not respect the rules, should be taken into custody by the military police if they were military men or by the civilian police, and that proceedings be instituted against them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the point I'm making, Dr. Mujezinovic, is that once that process had begun, once these people suspected of criminal activity had actually been apprehended, you and your colleagues on the war presidency relied upon the legal system to carry through to its end without intervening, yourselves; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If a soldier was in question, the soldiers were apprehended by the military police of the BH army. There was a military court in Zenica and a prison in Zenica, and they, the military court, conducted the proceedings against people suspected of having violated the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's exactly right, Dr. Mujezinovic. That's the point I'm making, that once these people had been made subjects of the criminal justice system, such as it existed, even in the military context, you left the administration of that process, the wheels of justice, so to speak, to move in their own way, without becoming involved yourself; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did not interfere in the work of the courts or their decisions. They had their own rules of procedure, and the court was independent of us. We couldn't have an influence over the decisions of the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is right, sir, and if you had tried to interfere or in any way monitor the progress of the criminal investigations, you would have been told that that's a matter for the criminal justice system and not a matter within your competence; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That was within the competence of the military or the civilian court. It was not within our sphere of competence. Our responsibility was to have all suspects apprehended and proceedings started against them. At the war presidency we had a very clear stand in that regard, because we really did wish to have peace restored, and we wanted to avoid conflict. We requested from the army commanders and the chiefs of the civilian police to strictly respect the rules of duty or, rather, the recommendations of the presidency and government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, I think we've covered the point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've testified about the most serious incident that you're aware of involving ABiH troops, an incident at which six HVO soldiers were beaten up shortly before the outbreak of the April 1993 hostilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of November, two soldiers of the BH army were killed on the road from Vitez to the village of Kruscica. One was called Huso Haric, and the other was, I think, Esad Mujo. We insisted, and orders were issued by the local commander, that the first HVO unit that arrives --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I don't mean to be impolite, but I just asked you if that was your testimony and not to repeat the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, you are not being impolite. It is the duty of counsel to control the witnesses. If there is some point on which you don't need the evidence, then it's your duty to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, the village of Dusina is just a few kilometres down the road from Vitez, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it is about 18 or 20 kilometres away. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that 13 Croat civilians had been massacred in the village of Dusina on January the 25th and 26th, 1993, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had heard about it, but I'm really not familiar with the details about Dusina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that three HVO officers and their driver had been kidnapped, supposedly by the 7th Muslim Brigade forces, on April the 14th, 1993, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. As far that case is concerned, there were such cases, but I'm not familiar with the details. I know what happened in Vitez. As for the broader region, I can just tell you what I had heard, that there were incidents in Travnik, Zenica -- you mentioned the village of Dusina, I mentioned the village of Kruscica -- Busovaca. There were incidents on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, turning to the last one of those incidents that I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to, you were aware that commander Zivko Totic had been kidnapped by the 7th Muslim Brigade in Zenica on April the 15th, 1993, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not see televised, sir, the pictures of commander Zivko Totic's bodyguard, consisting of three people, shot by approximately 100 bullets, shot to death in Zenica on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard later that some HVO soldiers had been killed in Zenica, but I really do not recollect that. I didn't see it, and nobody told me that Zivko Totic had been killed, and I don't know the man in person. I never met him. I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, in connection with the testimony that you gave regarding being driven back and forth between the Vitez health centre and your house after April the 19th, isn't it true that Dr. Bruno Buzuk, the health minister for the HVO, actually told you that that was occurring because of the danger of Muslim snipers shooting people in Vitez after April the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I was told by the driver who drove me -- I said that his name was Dragan Petrovic -- that he had received orders to drive me, but he didn't tell me anything about what you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that in 1993, five people were killed by sniper fire in Vitez and another 26 were wounded? Five Croats were killed and 26 Croats were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that from the 19th until I was exchanged, I had no contact, and all I knew was what I had heard from stories, but I didn't have any official data. I had no contact with the official representatives of the BH army. I really didn't know how many people were killed or wounded on either side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever treat either Marko Prskalo or Zoran Pilicic for gunshot wounds inflicted by snipers in the middle of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I said that there were many people wounded, especially after the 19th. I don't remember by name each of the wounded people who came for treatment. We had a registry where we entered the names and the diagnoses, the treatment we gave to each wounded person, whether he stayed on there or was sent to hospital, but I do not remember the names of all the individuals. I remember Ante Omazic, who was wounded in the stomach. I knew him well. We went to elementary school together. Whether it was from a sniper, I don't know. I remember him, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember treating either of the two gentlemen that I mentioned to you: Mr. Prskalo or Mr. Pililic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's possible that I may have treated them. I don't know. I told you I do not remember the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last series of questions on this particular subject, the people that you treated from April the 19th to May the 19th, 1993, you treated over 100 HVO soldiers who had been wounded and suffering from various types of injuries ranging from grave to light, and most inflicted by gunshot; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but they were wounds from firearms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me that you estimated that the number of people you treated on April the 19th alone was over 100 HVO troops suffering from various kinds of gunshot and explosion-related wounds; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The injuries were mostly from firearms, perhaps shrapnel. But in any event, from firearms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point I'm making is there were more than 100 on that day alone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness has said he doesn't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember being asked that precise question in the Blaskic case on August the 21st, 1997, sir? For my friend across the hall, it's at page 1783. The question was, "Can you estimate, were there more than 100?" Answer, "I think there were." Did you say that two years ago?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
