utterances.text: Possibly. I said that there were a large number of them, that I worked very hard, I worked all day, that I asked Dr. Buzuk to bring physicians who were capable, like Dr. Drago Moris, who was a surgeon, Dr. Patkovic, because there were indeed many. I repeat again, there may have been more than 100.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But you didn't treat any TO troops or troops from the ABiH. These were all, every single one of them, HVO troops; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final question, sir. Did I understand you to say, in your direct examination, that you had four hand grenades in your house on the evening of April the 15th, 1993; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of them. I said that my wife told me later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had four hand grenades in your house on the evening before the fighting broke out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is correct, but I was not aware of them. My neighbour from upstairs brought them and left them on the balcony. That's what my wife told me. Then my wife handed them in to Stipo Krizanac. I really didn't know about them, nor did I ever have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, just before you finish, the witness has said that Mr. Kordic was introduced to him as the first Croat of Central Bosnia, a colonel and the deputy president of the HZ-HB. Is it accepted that Mr. Kordic was introduced in those terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I really don't know, Your Honour, because I don't know what occasion the doctor was talking about. But I would be happy to cover that, if the Court wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Doctor, is that right, that the accused Mr. Kordic was introduced in those terms?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that he was introduced on the local public media, on television and the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. That's the answer. Now then, is that in dispute, that he was introduced in that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know the answer to that question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you ask Mr. Kordic then if it's disputed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I think that Mr. Kordic was introduced as a member of the HVO and he was introduced as a colonel, although he didn't wear any rank insignia, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Any re-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very little re-examination. But I have just a slight confusion as to the very last question that Mr. Sayers asked, the question about the hand grenades and, indeed, the questions of impeachment generally, because it's almost as if they are impregnated with another proposition, and the proposition isn't being advanced to the witness. I don't know what, if any, significance there is in them, and I can't deal with it. So far as re-examination is concerned, before I come to that, my attitude on Defence exhibits, as explained to Mr. Sayers, is this, so that the Trial Chamber understand: Obviously, I can't accept, certainly not at short notice, the prevalence of exhibits introduced in the defence of other cases. Equally, I can accept the prevalence of exhibits that come from our side. Of course I can. I simply ask if documents are put in, they are flagged up as to whether they are Defence exhibits in another case or where they come from. That's all. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, going back to questions you were asked on behalf of the defendant Cerkez, and deal with them as briefly as you can, before the war, his responsibilities in the factory, what were they, what did they include?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Cerkez worked in the department for self-protection and information in the work organisation SPS in Vitez. I think that he was in charge of materiel and technical resources in that work organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any, to your knowledge, weapons in that organisation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Cerkez was, in fact, in charge of the military supplies. In the work organisation, there was an entire service providing security for the plants, and these mainly contained military materiel; rifles, equipment, medical supplies for the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. You were asked about the HVO in Vitez having both military and civil authority. Was there any split in the chains of command or authority as between military and civil functions, to your knowledge, or not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what the chain of command and control was in the HVO. I learned that there was the staff of the HVO and the government of the HVO of Vitez, and our interpretation was that there was the civil part, the political part, that that was the government, and that the staff was the military part. I'm not sure of this, whether that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did Mr. Cerkez fit in, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Cerkez came as the commander of the HVO staff in Vitez. He would occasionally attend meetings of the crisis staff, as necessary. And Marijan Skopljak also came, Hakija Cengic, and later Sefkija Djidic, when there were any disagreements between the HVO and the TO, which later became the BH army, at the local level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had authority to speak for the HVO military side at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mostly, it was Mario Cerkez who spoke, and Marijan Skopljak. For a while, he was the Defence minister, Stipo Krizanac, but later on, Marijan Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of Cerkez and Skopljak, who was senior?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know. I'm not conversant with that hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the way people were introduced, for example, on television. The question related to Kraljevic, but you've also spoken of Kordic. Was Mr. Cerkez ever the subject of television information, and if so, how was he announced?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I never listened to that. He may have been, probably, but I never heard Mario Cerkez on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next topic is something that I may be able to deal with very briefly. Mr. Sayers suggests that the Tribunal has a collection of this witness's witness statements. I wasn't sure if that was the case or not. If you have them, I can deal with it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The answer is that the legal officer has a collection. We don't, individually, have a collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I deal with this topic very briefly, and if my friends opposite want me to deal with it in more detail, they must say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of your four statements, the first in 1995, do you recall that that was -- I'm going to lead on this -- that that was something that has never been signed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, because I wasn't happy about the translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The remaining three statements, each of which has been signed, were they taken in English or in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Questions were asked of me in English, and I had an interpreter. I really was not satisfied with the manner, and on one occasion I asked them to find another interpreter here in the Tribunal from Mr. McNowell from the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first have a chance to see the translations from English into your own language of these statements, or any of them, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was usually a day or two after I had given a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to one topic that you were asked about by Mr. Kovacic, you were asked about the conversation in the car with Kraljevic, in which you told the Court that he mentioned Cerkez, along with Skopljak and Santic, and you were asked about the fact that you had not mentioned that, I think, in a later statement or testimony. Is it the case, and again I'm going to lead this, that on page 12 of your first signed statement, the 13th and 16th of July of 1995, that you mentioned that Cerkez, along with Valenta, Skopljak, and Santic, were spoken of by Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mentioned -- first of all, I said that the most persistent in all this were Anto Valenta and Pero Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, I'm going to cut you again short. The question is susceptible to a "Yes"/"No" answer. Is it right that in that statement, the first signed statement, you mentioned Cerkez, along with the other three? Just "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were shown yesterday -- no. Staying with that topic, you have been asked a number of questions about what you said of Kraljevic. An extract was provided of part of your testimony in Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to fill in the blanks, although it may be that it's sometimes a slightly unfortunate course to extract passages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case that in addition to whatever you saw of Kraljevic, you also had information about use of drugs, maybe in the form of gossip but from others, not necessarily in relation to him but in relation to troops generally?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was talk about that in Vitez, that HOS formations were distributing drugs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: But this is purely gossip. I did not see it. I do not know if that was true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave an account to the Tribunal, in answer to questions from me, of your judgement of the lucidity, the clarity, of what Kraljevic was saying when he spoke of Valenta, Skopljak, Santic, and Cerkez. You gave that evidence last week, I think. In light of what you've been asked by the Defence, do you want to change that, or is your evidence unchanged on that topic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: During our conversation in the car, he spoke normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything you want to change from what you first told the Chamber last week?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to try to correct. It is either an error or it was misleading. I think it's better to do it now than on the end of the testimony. The Prosecutor was asking about the first statement of the witness and then was referring to the date 16 May, 1995. That is not correct. We had been talking, when I asked the witness on that, the first statement is on the 1st March '95, and in that one, he never mentioned Cerkez. It would be better to clear it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think on every occasion, I said it was the first signed statement, and I've distinguished between the unsigned statement and the signed one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if any, changes do you want to make in the account that you gave to the Chamber last week as to the clarity of speech of Kraljevic in the car?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He spoke normally while we talked, and what do I know? He wasn't showing any signs of aggression. It was just a chat, a conversation between two persons. He was asking me about my opinion, and I advised him to leave Vitez. I mean --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've been asked about the HOS and the Vitezovi, into which it changed. Just remind us, please, what sort of period you're dealing with, the change from HOS to Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was the latter half of '92.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Darko Kraljevic in charge of the Vitezovi from then and until the time of your escape, or your exchange? I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I stated that on the local television, he was introduced as colonel and as the commander of the special unit, Vitezovi, HVO Vitezovi, special HVO formation called Vitezovi, with the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anything said to you or did anybody else say to you about the lines of command of the Vitezovi and how it connected or otherwise with other parts of the HVO in Vitez or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally on the subject of Kraljevic, who is dead, is he commemorated in Vitez, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really don't know. I've passed through by car. I know there is a monument in Vitez to him. There was flowers and wreaths there. But as I don't live and don't work in Vitez and I don't really go to Vitez at all, I just don't know. I don't have any latest information about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. There was a video shown yesterday with an untranslated transcript. It showed you in hospital in April. It's hard for you to remember this, but was there anything on that soundtrack that needed translating or that you want to draw to our attention? I have to ask it this way because we haven't had any other opportunity of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I was brought there to work, escorted by military police, and I truly worked there and I did all that was within my power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was, was there anything said on the soundtrack that you think may assist us?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In this -- on this soundtrack, I stated that it had been said that I had been killed, and I said, "Well, don't you see that I'm working here?" I introduced other doctors who had been brought to work here, and they were both Muslims and Croats, and there was a lady doctor, Serb, and also a male Serb doctor. I was simply trying to allay the tension, to show that the picture was not as black as it was usually reported to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke of a television interview where you were invited to say things but you declined, as I've understood it. What were you being invited at one stage to say that you were not prepared to say?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was asked to invite Muslims from Stari Vitez to lay down their weapons, and that was what I declined to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This morning, you were shown one document only that I want you to look at, and again very briefly. It's D20/2, and it's my mistake probably for not understanding something. On the top -- for public display, this would actually require the original to be shown on the ELMO, if at all, but on the top we see two figures number 1. We've got a translation of the top one of those. First of all, had you seen this document, or any part of it, before you were shown it this morning?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The writing, apart from the signature at the foot, do you recognise it at all?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I see this document. I mean I saw it today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to help -- probably the answer is self-evident, but I must ask it. Are you able to help, one way or another, with why the top entry on the page has been written above by a further top entry given number 1? Can you offer any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. Mensus Aganovic, Rasim's son, I do not know that man at all. It says here that he went home, and somebody's signature, but I simply cannot identify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You were asked questions about your motivation for leaving Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice that no alternative explanation was ventured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about having the courage to leave Vitez or how you had the courage to leave Vitez. Did you want to leave your family at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think really the time may be coming to bring this to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I've got one other question or two other questions of substance to deal with, but I've been very brief, as Your Honour will note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Doctor, are you all right? Would you like a break? Are there --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They are questions of importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you, Doctor, deal with one question, and then we'll release you, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are two or three questions, and they relate to the role of --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- Dr. Mujezinovic in relation to the army and his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, you've been asked about troops from Santici, Ahmici, and Pirici fighting on the front lines, but just help us with this. In the middle of April of 1993, were there any BiH units stationed at or in any of those villages?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been asked about your knowledge of the deployment of forces. Were those villages defended in any way at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your role, you had knowledge of the deployment of troops and of the movement of soldiers. Did you have any part of direction or control over the soldiers yourself, any direct control over the movement of BiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had to know where the army was, how many soldiers there were, how many of them were on the ground. I had to be aware of the orders they received from the superior command. The war presidency had to know this, this kind of thing, that is, have all the information related to armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any, yourself, ability directly to control the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Through commanders who were responsible for individual units, and it was through them that we exercised our influence, that is, those commanders, upon receiving orders from us, first had to obey their superiors or, rather, seek approval for what we were asking them to do. In other words, we did have some influence as regards the appointment and requests of commanders of individual formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes all I want to ask of this witness, with apologies for having dealt with matters so briskly, maybe, that I lacked some sensitivity at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, thank you for coming to the Tribunal for giving evidence, and thank you for giving evidence. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, if I may, I should like to say two sentences only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Provided they are relevant, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I believe they are. First, I was really surprised when the Prosecutor commented on some questions asked by the Defence. I find that unnecessary, because I believe that the Court will evaluate what we did. But that was only by the way. The important thing which I wish to clarify here is the following: What my colleague Steve Sayers said, he agreed with the Prosecution about the document that we tendered; the Prosecutor did not respond to that, which means that he agreed to that. However, if I understand him properly, now, in the end, the Prosecutor expressed a certain degree of reservation as regards those documents. Now the question arises: Were these documents admitted on the basis of the consent of the two parties or not? That is the only point that I wish clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suggest that be a matter for consultation between the parties. If the Prosecution have got submissions about the documents, then they could make them in due course. I say that because apparently there was no notice given that these documents were about to be adduced. And if that is going to happen, it places on the party, the other party, a very real difficulty. And in those circumstances, I would allow the Prosecution time to make submissions on the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that. I'm equally happy to make my position plain, as I made it plain to Mr. Sayers at the break. In relation to all the documents that have been put in by the Defence, I have raised, I think, no objection to any document. Objections take time, and it is far better that if they want you to see a document, you should see it, and we can work out its value later. I simply made the point, but of course, if a document comes from the Defence in another trial, I'm in no position to concede its genuineness, either on short notice or necessarily at any stage. We simply need to know, for later appraisal, where documents come from -- and I asked Mr. Sayers, and as I understood it, he was happy about this -- that Defence exhibits should simply be flagged as Defence exhibits. Before the next witness comes, may we go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we do, there is something I want to say. We would have all seen the distress of that last witness. You, Mr. Nice, apologised. In my judgement, of course, you were right to do so. There was no need to do so. It was not the briskness of the questioning which I suspect caused the distress; it was the length that the witness had been giving evidence. The Bench is most concerned about this, that a witness was brought here last week; he gives evidence -- this is the third or fourth time, it doesn't matter -- in the Tribunal, and in this case, he's kept here for two and a half days. We must speed up the way in which the evidence is given, and -- well, it may be premature, but for the next witness, we are going to suggest targets in order that we get through this witness and the next one by the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Excellent. I'm grateful to Your Honour for mentioning that. May I -- and I don't want to rub salt into what may be a small wound at the moment on the opposite side, but of course the topic that caused distress was the topic about which questions had been asked but not focused, and I simply needed to know where I stood, but there it is. I think Mr. Kovacic wants to raise something, but if we may go into closed session for the next witness -- not for the next witness; before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- he comes to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I wanted to say something else that we unwittingly opened here. I think we are faced now with a problem that we may have to face again, so I'm trying to be constructive. During his examination of Mr. Mujezinovic, Mr. Nice disqualified the first statement that the witness gave, saying that it was not signed. Now, if we begin to use statements that were adduced as part of supporting material because allegedly they had not been signed, then the question arises as to the justification of the confirmation of the indictments, because these statements are found in the supporting material, and the Tribunal confirmed the indictments on the basis of that material, and now, when this is taken out as an exhibit and shown to the witness, then we say "Well, it's no go, because it's not been signed." I'm afraid it might have some very undesirable consequences, so that I'm suggesting that we resolve this matter in principle. Evidently these statements that were given by witnesses to investigators are not evidence, and I don't really think that it really matters very much whether it was signed or not. It was a statement made by a witness, and we simply are trying to clarify the validity of that statement, juxtaposing it to what the statement (sic) testified here, giving evidence. If that is the approach, that may be all right, but if we are changing this approach, then we really have a problem, because evidently the material adduced was not legally valid, and this is not the only such case; this is only one of the examples. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, the only significance of the questioning about whether the statement was signed was this, that questions were put to the witness about something he said in the statement, and therefore his credit was being in that way impeached or attacked. If that is done, and the witness said that he complained about the translation, it is relevant as to whether the statement was signed or not. Apart from that, there is no significance in the questioning. So if there is a question about a statement, and the witness gives answers about it, it is relevant to know -- or it may be relevant -- to know whether the statement has been signed or not. It's not evidence; it's merely a question of whether his credit could be impeached because of what's in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to settle Mr. Kovacic's concern -- I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, I absolutely agree. That is what I had in mind, and I wouldn't like us to debate this example, but it is a fact that we do have unsigned statements, and bona fide, at the cross, I asked the witness whether he had said what he said. I didn't enter into a debate as to whether there was a signature or not. And today the Prosecutor explained by the lack of signature the fact that we were engaging in this impeachment procedure. So we no longer have equal arms, because the explanation is precisely what you have given. We are treating it in the way we are. We can't just say, "This is not signed, so it's not in debate any more," because the indictment is based on it. So in that case, let us eliminate all the statements that have no signature. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On this topic, we want to make it plain that the question whether a statement is signed or not is something that we will be considering when we look at the evidence and decide what weight to put upon the particular point. That, in my judgement, is the only significance of it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, now, closed session -- yes, Mr. Stein. What do you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'll be succinct. The next witness who is proffered, whose statements you may have read -- and this foreshadows this afternoon -- is going to testify far and wide in range about towns not named in the indictments, about issues not in the indictment, and to the extent that even we have from the Prosecutor this morning a summary of his testimony, or a road map through his testimony, of some 17 pages, most of it again tracks what we've seen in the discovery, and the lion's share of it simply will not advance the cause. To this regard, I suggest that the Tribunal limit the testimony to the length -- I suggest the Tribunal limit the testimony to what this witness has to offer about these two defendants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, he is entitled to deal -- are you saying he is not entitled to deal with any area? Kresevo, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Kresevo is not named in the indictment, it's not a town at issue, nor are the other towns that are mentioned in his summaries. They are not specific named towns set out in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe go into closed session first, because the whole question of publicity of this witness has to be dealt with first. As that is being organised, may I, before I overlook the point, hark back for one sentence to console Mr. Kovacic over his concern over the unsigned statement. The unsigned statement was not submitted at either the time of the confirmation of the original or the amended indictment, and that's shown up on the witness confidential list. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 4.34 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of May, 1999, at 9.45 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
